title: BuzzFeed, Inc. Reports Q2 2026 Financial Results
summary: NEW YORK --(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 4, 2026-- BuzzFeed, Inc. (“BuzzFeed” or the “Company”) (Nasdaq: BZFD) today announced its financial results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026. “BuzzFeed, Tasty, and HuffPost are strong, recognizable brands that have loyal users, but we made it clear on our last
body_text: PDF Version NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 4, 2026-- BuzzFeed, Inc. (“BuzzFeed” or the “Company”) (Nasdaq: BZFD) today announced its financial results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026. “BuzzFeed, Tasty, and HuffPost are strong, recognizable brands that have loyal users, but we made it clear on our last earnings call that these businesses were carrying an unsustainable cost structure, and a restructure was immediately needed,” said Byron Allen, BuzzFeed Chairman and CEO . “As such, we recently took steps to significantly reduce costs to better align our cost base with the underlying business, giving us the foundation to grow. I’m also excited to share that BuzzFeed has entered into a sales representation agreement with Allen Media Group (“AMG”), engaging AMG’s sales organization to expand monetization of BuzzFeed’s advertising inventory and give brands and agencies another point of entry to build campaigns spanning premium television, streaming, local broadcast, and digital-first media. I’m energized by what we’re building at BuzzFeed, and by the path we’re now on towards sustainable profitability, positive cash flow, and disciplined investment in our highest-growth priorities.” “The changes we’ve made create the opportunity to build BuzzFeed differently,” said Jonah Peretti, President of BuzzFeed AI . “We’re shifting from a traditional publishing model to a true platform – one where our community, creators, and partners actively fuel our content ecosystem. That means a more flexible operating model in editorial, and new AI-supported tools in tech that keep human creativity at the core. This operational discipline gives us runway to innovate, transform, and build our next chapter.” Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Operational Highlights BuzzFeed delivered Q2 2026 revenues of $36.3 million, declining 21.8% compared to the second quarter of 2025 Advertising revenue declined 23.4% year-over-year to $17.3 million. Content revenue declined 6.5% year-over-year to $10.0 million. Commerce and other revenue declined 31.4% year-over-year to $9.0 million. Net loss was $11.8 million, compared to a net loss of $10.6 million in Q2 2025. Adjusted EBITDA 1 was negative $1.7 million for Q2 2026, compared to positive $2.0 million in Q2 2025. In Q2 2026, audience Time Spent 2 with our content totaled 62.3 million hours, reflecting an approximately 10.8% decline compared to Q2 2025. Business and Content Highlights BuzzFeed, the Company’s largest brand, maintained its position as the #1 brand in total U.S. time spent among any single media brand in its competitive set3, reaching 36.0 million hours in Q2 2026. This significantly outpaced second-place People at 26.4 million hours. HuffPost recorded 18.0 million hours in total U.S. time spent in Q2 2026, up 16% from last quarter, significantly outperforming competitors such as Vogue.com (4.1 million hours), The New Yorker (3.6 million hours), New York Magazine (2.6 million hours), Vanity Fair (1.9 million hours), Vox.com (0.9 million hours), and Bustle.com (0.5 million hours). Direct visits and internal web and app referrals have taken up 65% of the U.S. traffic on BuzzFeed’s owned and operated properties, an increase from 61% from the prior quarter, reducing the brand’s reliance on distributed platforms and increasing its resilience to platform algorithm changes. First Half 2026 Results Total revenue declined 17.7% to $67.9 million. Net loss increased 16.8% to $27.0 million. Adjusted EBITDA loss increased by $5.6 million to negative $9.5 million. Full Year 2026 Financial Outlook Given the transformation underway, we are focused on full-year operational targets rather than quarterly guidance. As the restructuring and platform transition progresses, we expect to provide investors with a more complete financial outlook. Quarterly Conference Call BuzzFeed’s management team will hold a conference call to discuss our second quarter 2026 results today, August 4, at 5 PM ET. The call will be available via webcast at investors.buzzfeed.com under the heading News and Events, and parties interested in participating must register in advance at the same location. Upon registration, all telephone participants will receive a confirmation email detailing how to join the conference call, including the dial-in number along with a unique PIN that can be used to access the call. While it is not required, it is recommended you join 5 minutes prior to the event start time. A replay of the call will be made available at the same URL. We have used, and intend to continue to use, the Investor Relations section of our website at investors.buzzfeed.com as a means of disclosing material nonpublic information and for complying with our disclosure obligations under Regulation FD. Definitions BuzzFeed reports revenues across three primary business lines: Advertising, Content, and Commerce and other. The definition of “ Time Spent ” is also set forth below. Advertising revenues are primarily generated from advertisers, both programmatically and directly, for ads distributed against our editorial and news content, including display, pre-roll and mid-roll video products. We distribute these ad products across our owned and operated sites as well as third-party platforms, primarily YouTube and Apple News. Content revenues are primarily generated from clients for custom assets, including both long-form and short-form content, from branded quizzes to Instagram takeovers to sponsored content. Studio generally includes revenue from films, micro-dramas, content licensing, TV projects, and other projects inspired by BuzzFeed IP. Commerce and other revenues consist primarily of affiliate commissions earned on transactions initiated from our editorial shopping content. Revenues from our product licensing businesses are also included here. Time Spent captures the time audiences spend engaging with our content across our owned and operated sites, as well as YouTube and Apple News, as measured by Comscore. This metric excludes time spent with our content on platforms for which we have minimal advertising capabilities that contribute to our Advertising revenues, including Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, Snapchat, and X (formerly Twitter). There are inherent challenges in measuring the total actual number of hours spent with our content across all platforms; however, we consider the data reported by Comscore to represent industry-standard estimates of the time actually spent on our largest distribution platforms with our most significant monetization opportunities. About BuzzFeed, Inc. BuzzFeed, Inc. is home to the best of the Internet. Across pop culture, entertainment, shopping, food, and news, our brands drive conversation and inspire what audiences watch, read, and buy now — and into the future. Born on the Internet in 2006, BuzzFeed is committed to making it better: providing trusted, quality, brand-safe news and entertainment to hundreds of millions of people; making content on the Internet more inclusive, empathetic, and creative; and inspiring our audience to live better lives. Non-GAAP Financial Measures Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA margin are non-GAAP financial measures and represent key metrics used by management and our board of directors to measure the operational strength and performance of our business, to establish budgets, and to develop operational goals for managing our business. body_text: A Minnesota woman who was hospitalized with sepsis after developing a severe Salmonella infection has filed a lawsuit against Chipotle, claiming that contaminated jalapeño peppers in a burrito bowl caused her illness. The lawsuit comes as federal health officials investigate a Salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeño peppers sourced from Mexico. According to health authorities, hundreds of people across the United States have been infected with the outbreak strain, with dozens requiring hospitalization. Minnesota woman files lawsuit against Chipotle Kristen Behne, a Minnesota resident, says she became seriously ill after eating at a Chipotle restaurant in Roseville, Minnesota, on June 24. According to the lawsuit, Behne began experiencing symptoms several days later, including fever, chills, and vomiting. Her condition reportedly worsened rapidly, and she eventually developed severe diarrhea and sepsis. Her attorneys claim that laboratory testing found Salmonella in Behne that matched the strain associated with the ongoing outbreak. The lawsuit alleges that the food she consumed at Chipotle contained jalapeño peppers connected to the Salmonella outbreak. It seeks more than $75,000 in compensatory damages. The allegations have not been proven in court, and Chipotle has not been found legally responsible for Behne's illness. Salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeño peppers The lawsuit comes amid a broader Salmonella investigation involving jalapeño peppers distributed to restaurants across the United States. Federal health officials have reported 345 illnesses across 27 states as of August 5, with 36 people hospitalized. Minnesota and Colorado have reported some of the highest numbers of cases. No deaths connected to the outbreak had been reported as of the latest federal data cited in the report. The Food and Drug Administration has said the illnesses were associated with jalapeño peppers sourced from Mexico. Investigators also found that many people who became sick reported eating at Mexican restaurants before developing symptoms. According to federal investigators, approximately 93 percent of nearly 200 interviewed patients said they had eaten at a Mexican restaurant before becoming ill. Restaurants mentioned in connection with the investigation include Chipotle and Qdoba. Severe symptoms reported in Chipotle lawsuit The lawsuit describes a rapid progression of illness after Behne's reported Chipotle meal. According to her attorneys, she began experiencing fever, chills, and vomiting on June 27. She reportedly lost consciousness and developed a temperature of approximately 102 degrees Fahrenheit. The following day, the lawsuit says she experienced more than 10 episodes of diarrhea within 24 hours. Behne was subsequently admitted to a hospital on June 28. She was discharged two days later, according to the complaint. Her lawyers say that she continues to experience effects associated with the Salmonella infection and the septic episode. The lawsuit also claims that she could face an increased risk of complications, including reactive arthritis and post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome. What is Salmonella? Salmonella is a type of bacteria that can cause foodborne illness. Infection commonly results from consuming contaminated food or water, although transmission can also occur through contact with infected people or animals. Typical Salmonella symptoms include diarrhea, abdominal cramps and fever. Nausea, vomiting, chills and headache can also occur. Many people recover without serious complications. However, some infections can become severe, particularly when bacteria spread beyond the digestive system. Sepsis is one of the potentially life-threatening complications that can occur when the body's response to an infection becomes extreme and causes organ dysfunction. People experiencing severe symptoms, dehydration, persistent high fever, bloody diarrhea, confusion or other signs of serious illness should seek urgent medical attention. Chipotle says affected peppers were removed Chipotle has said that protecting the health and safety of customers and employees is its highest priority. The company stated that it has a system designed to trace ingredients through its supply chain. After learning about a potential Salmonella outbreak affecting wholesalers and restaurants, Chipotle said it identified the potentially affected jalapeño peppers and removed them from restaurants where they had been distributed. The company also said it replaced the peppers with products from different growers. Chipotle reportedly changed its jalapeño supplier for affected restaurants beginning July 20. Qdoba also stopped serving the peppers approximately a week later. Federal officials have said they do not currently believe there is an ongoing risk associated with the affected jalapeños at Chipotle and Qdoba because the restaurants removed the potentially contaminated products. What customers should know about the outbreak The investigation highlights the difficulty consumers face when dealing with foodborne pathogens. Salmonella contamination cannot necessarily be detected by looking at or smelling food. Contaminated food may appear normal, making it difficult for customers to identify a potential problem before eating it. Health officials continue to investigate the source and distribution of the contaminated peppers as they monitor reported illnesses. Consumers who believe they may have developed Salmonella after eating at a restaurant should contact a healthcare professional, particularly if symptoms are severe or persistent. People who become seriously ill may also want to keep records of where and when they ate, their symptoms, medical treatment and any relevant receipts or other documentation. Such records can be important during public health investigations or potential legal proceedings. Lawsuit alleges Chipotle was responsible Behne's legal complaint argues that she reasonably relied on Chipotle to provide food that was safe to eat. Her attorneys contend that she could not have detected Salmonella in the food herself because the bacteria cannot be identified simply by looking at, smelling or tasting a contaminated ingredient. The lawsuit therefore seeks compensation for the consequences the plaintiff says resulted from her infection, hospitalization and septic episode. However, filing a lawsuit does not establish that the allegations are true. Chipotle may contest the claims, and the legal process will determine whether the company can be held responsible for the illness described in the complaint. The broader food safety concern The Chipotle case is part of a wider series of foodborne illness investigations affecting restaurants in the United States. The current Salmonella investigation involving jalapeño peppers has raised concerns about how contaminated ingredients can move through complex food supply chains before the source of an outbreak is identified. Restaurants and food suppliers rely on traceability systems to identify potentially affected products and remove them from circulation. When contamination is discovered, rapid action can help reduce the risk of additional infections. For consumers, the outbreak is also a reminder that foodborne illness can sometimes develop into a serious medical emergency. As federal agencies continue investigating the Salmonella outbreak, additional information could emerge about the source of the contaminated peppers, the distribution chain, and the restaurants that received affected products. Frequently Asked Questions What caused the Salmonella outbreak? Federal health officials have linked the current outbreak to jalapeño peppers sourced from Mexico. Investigators are continuing to examine the distribution of the affected products. How many people have been affected? According to the federal health data cited in the report, 345 people in 27 states had been infected with the outbreak strain, with 36 hospitalizations reported as of August 5, 2026. Did Chipotle cause the woman's Salmonella infection? The lawsuit alleges that Behne became infected after eating a Chipotle burrito bowl containing outbreak-linked jalapeño peppers. This remains an allegation and has not been established as a legal finding. What are common Salmonella symptoms? Common symptoms include diarrhea, stomach cramps, and fever. Some people can develop more serious complications requiring hospitalization. Is there still a risk from the affected peppers at Chipotle? Federal officials said they do not believe there is an ongoing risk from the affected jalapeños at Chipotle and Qdoba because the restaurants removed the potentially contaminated products and changed suppliers.
